 Subscribe Home Our Region Business Sports Steelers Food & Drink Obituaries Public Notices PGe Edition Breaking Pittsburgh Carnegie museum receives $5M gift and 3 rare dinosaurs from Ken Griffin 
 Mary Ann Thomas 11/18/2026 9:30 a.m. EST Share Share this via... The commercial paleontology lab Fossilogic LLC excavated one adult and three juvenile sauropod dinosaurs in Washakie County, Wyoming between 2023 and 2025. ( Sotheby’s & Fossilogic LLC ) ‘This is a chance for people to see something they have not seen before’
 Three dinosaurs are soon to be Pittsburgh bound, with their extraction from sediment to be on display after they land at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History. 
 Philanthropist Ken Griffin, who donated $3 billion to CMU in September, has donated $5 million and loaned the three rare sauropods — possibly a family — to the Carnegie, the museum announced on Wednesday.
 Griffin, the founder and CEO of investment firm Citadel, is the 37th richest person in the world. He also founded Griffin Catalyst , a civic engagement initiative embodying his philanthropic and community efforts.
 He has bought fossils and a dinosaur cast before and supported museums for their display, research and public education.
 Advertise with us The $5 million gift to the Carnegie museum will expand paleontological research, educational programming and public engagement, including through upgraded museum facilities.
 The dinosaurs being loaned to the Carnegie — an adult and two juveniles — were fossilized together in Wyoming’s geologic Morrison Formation . The site’s origins began 157–150 million years ago and is famous for other dinosaur finds from the Jurassic period.
 The commercial paleontology lab Fossilogic excavated the dinosaurs in Washakie County, Wyoming, between 2023 and 2025. 
 The fossils, many of which are still embedded in rock, will be shipped in pieces in December or January. The Carnegie Museum of Natural History will add staff, courtesy of Griffin’s donation, to extract the fossils from sediment in a lab visible to the public.
 “We have been entrusted with something rare and exciting to study, possibly a family of dinosaurs that isn’t behind closed doors,” said Carey Scheide Miller, Daniel G. and Carole L. Kamin Director of the Carnegie Museum of Natural History and vice president of Carnegie Museums
 Advertise with us “This is a chance for people to see something they have not seen before,” she said in an interview with the Post-Gazette.
 Griffin is loaning the fossils for a decade and covering the costs for fossil preparation, which includes adding five full-time staff and two interns to the museum’s paleontology department.
 Griffin was drawn to the Carnegie’s internationally renowned expertise in sauropods, Miller said.
 Dippy , whose real name is Diplodocus carnegii, is a sauropod and is among the world’s largest dinosaurs. It was named after Andrew Carnegie because he funded an expedition to find the specimen, which has been replicated for museums the world over.
 Dippy the dinosaur at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Oakland. (Esteban Marenco/Pittsburgh Post-Gazette) The Carnegie has been working with Griffin’s team for more than a year on the donation. “They understood our sauropod research and paleontology is world class,” Miller said.
 Advertise with us The three Griffin dinosaurs, named Daisy, Lucky and Lucy, are sauropods — plant-eating, long-necked reptiles in the same family as Dippy, the can’t-miss 80-foot-long dinosaur with its own statue sitting outside of the Carnegie in Oakland. 
 The fossils include perhaps the largest sample of sauropod skin found to date.
 Griffin approached the museum with the three fossils and agreed to a 10-year loan to complete excavation of the bones in a display area for the public to watch. Then the bones will be assembled and mounted for an exhibit at the museum, for about five years.
 “Daisy, Lucky, and Lucy offer an extraordinary window into our planet’s history,” said Kenneth C. Griffin in a press release. 
 “I am proud to partner with the Carnegie Museum of Natural History to share these remarkable dinosaurs with the public and give visitors a front-row seat to the work of paleontologists. I hope these experiences spark curiosity and inspire the next generation of scientists,” he said.
 Advertise with us Griffin bought Apex , the Stegosaurus fossil, for $44.6 million in 2024. It is on loan to the American Museum of Natural History in New York, where Griffin is supporting scientists to study the dinosaur’s biology and life history.
 In 2017, Griffin donated a touchable cast of a 122-foot long titanosaur as part of a $16.5 million gift to the Field Museum in Chicago.
 Citadel CEO Ken Griffin speaks at CMU's Tepper School of Business in Oakland during an event to announce his $3 billion gift to the school on Sept. 30. (Alexandra Wimley/Pittsburgh Post-Gazette) The Carnegie’s upcoming exhibit of Griffin’s trio of dinosaurs — from the same species from a single quarry — is uncommon, according to Miller.
 The new dinosaur adult is between 80 to 100 feet long and the juveniles are 18 feet long, she said.
 “These are very large dinosaurs, and they will be in our museum. It will be a huge draw.”
 Advertise with us There are at least 120 bones for Daisy, the adult sauropod (it’s unknown if it’s a female) and about 150 bones from the two young sauropods that have been excavated so far.
 Three dinosaurs from the Jurassic Period found in Wyoming will be extracted from rock in real time before the public at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History. (Sotheby’s and Dr. Scott Hartman) Griffin’s donation supports more than preparing fossils: It will expand educational opportunities for the public and expand the paleontology lab, which will be named after Griffin, Miller said.
 Excavating the prehistoric creatures could take an estimated five years, she said. Paleontology educators will be stationed at the public-facing paleontology lab to answer questions and update visitors in real time while the fossils are extracted.
 “We would not have been able to do this without the additional support and preparation from Mr. Griffin,” Miller said.
 The plans are for the museum to enlarge and update the paleontology lab to show fossil preparation.
 Advertise with us “Mr. Griffin’s support for Carnegie Museum of Natural History will advance world-class scientific research, enrich educational experiences for our visitors and reinforce Pittsburgh’s standing as a global center of discovery, learning, and innovation,” said Steven Knapp, president and CEO of Carnegie Museums.
 To learn more about when the public can see museum staff working on the dinosaur fossils, consult the museum’s website and social media channels.
 Mary Ann Thomas 
 mthomas@post-gazette.com 
 Mary Ann Thomas is a Post-Gazette features and outdoors reporter. A Pittsburgh native and University of Pittsburgh graduate, she has spent more than two decades covering regional news including research on the flora and fauna of Western Pennsylvania.
